narration.text: This unit begins with how to drive through work zones and then turns to regulatory signs, the signs that state laws you must obey. The manual asks you to give construction workers a brake by slowing down in work zones and being ready to stop suddenly, and it tells you not to tailgate there. A driver who endangers a highway worker may be fined and have points added to the driving record. Regulatory signs are white with black, red or green letters or symbols, and they cover matters such as traffic direction, lane use, turning, speed and parking.

lines.text: Slow down, be ready to stop
Fines and points for endangering workers

narration.text: The manual's phrase for work zone conduct is to give construction workers a brake. That means slowing down in work zones and being ready to stop suddenly. It also means not tailgating other vehicles while you are in a work zone, because the vehicle ahead may have to stop suddenly too. These rules protect the people working on the road. A driver who endangers a highway worker may be fined and may also have points added to their driving record under state law, so both the fine and the points can follow a single careless moment in a work zone.

narration.text: Regulatory signs are square, rectangular or a special shape, and they are white with black, red or green letters or symbols. Their job is to state specific laws you must obey, covering matters such as traffic direction, lane use, turning, speed and parking. That sets them apart from signs that only give information or warnings. The manual pictures common regulatory signs including No U-Turn, No Left Turn, No Right Turn, Left Turn Only, Straight, and Straight or Turn Right. Each of these states a rule for what you may or may not do at that spot.

lines.text: Red circle with a red slash

narration.text: Some regulatory signs show a red circle with a red slash across a symbol, and that combination prohibits the action pictured. So a left-turn arrow under a red circle and slash means no left turn, and a U-turn arrow under it means no U-turn. Regulatory signs in general state laws you must follow, while the version with a red circle and slash specifically forbids whatever action is pictured beneath it. When you see that red circle and slash, the question is simple: the action shown inside it is the one you may not do at that location.

Here is a trap. Speed limit signs are black and white and give the maximum legal speed allowed in ideal conditions. Because the number is posted, some drivers treat it as the right speed at all times. But the limit is a maximum, and it applies in ideal conditions. Speed limit signs set a maximum that applies in ideal conditions, so they are not a guarantee that the posted speed is safe at every moment. When conditions are not ideal, the posted number remains the most you may legally drive, not a speed you are entitled to keep.

narration.text: This unit covers two of the most important regulatory signs, the stop sign and the yield sign, along with two signs about lane use. A stop sign is red with white letters and has eight sides. A yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing downward with red letters. You will learn where to stop at a stop sign, what to do after stopping, what a yield sign requires, how the Shared Center Lane Left Turn Only sign works and what one-way street signs tell you. Each sign gives a clear instruction about who moves and where.

title.text: Stopping point at a stop sign

lines.text: Behind the stop line or crosswalk
No line: closest point with a clear view

narration.text: At a stop sign you stop behind the stop line, or behind the crosswalk if there is one. Where a stop sign has no stop line, stop at the point closest to the intersection from which you can see both ways without pulling into the cross traffic lane. So the painted line comes first, then the crosswalk, and only when neither is present do you choose the closest spot with a clear view. In every case the goal is the same: you must be stopped before the intersection, at a point where you can see the traffic you are about to cross.

Stopping is only the first part of what a stop sign requires. After stopping at a stop sign, look in all directions for crossing vehicles and pedestrians and yield the right-of-way. A stop sign requires a stop and then yielding, so a full stop followed by an immediate start without looking does not meet the rule. Check both ways for crossing vehicles, check for pedestrians in or near your path, and let anyone with the right-of-way go first. Only then do you move into the intersection from the stopping point you chose behind the line, the crosswalk or the clear-view spot.

lines.text: Downward triangle: slow and give way

narration.text: Here is the trap. Stop signs and yield signs are both red and white, so they are easy to confuse. The stop sign is a red octagon with white letters, while the yield sign is a downward-pointing red and white triangle whose letters are red. Their duties differ too. A stop sign requires a stop and then yielding, whereas a yield sign requires slowing and letting right-of-way traffic cross before you enter. So at a yield sign you slow down and give way, stopping only if traffic with the right-of-way is crossing, while at a stop sign you always stop.

lines.text: Slow down and let traffic cross

narration.text: A yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing downward with red letters. It means slow down and let traffic that has the right-of-way cross before you enter. The shape is unique: no other sign in this section is a downward-pointing triangle, so you can recognize it even from the back or at a distance. Once you see it, reduce your speed and look for traffic that has the right-of-way. If that traffic is crossing, let it pass before you enter. If the way is clear, you may continue without a full stop, as the yield sign requires slowing rather than always stopping.

lines.text: Center lane: left turns from either direction

narration.text: The Shared Center Lane Left Turn Only sign marks a lane reserved for vehicles turning left from either direction, and it is not for through traffic or for passing. So drivers going both ways share that center lane, and only to make left turns. One-way street signs show that traffic moves only in the arrow's direction, so never turn against the arrow or drive the wrong way on a one-way street. Both signs tell you something about direction: the center lane is shared by both directions for turning, while a one-way street carries traffic in a single direction only.

The answer is at the point closest to the intersection from which you can see both ways without pulling into the cross traffic lane. If there were a stop line, you would stop behind it, or behind the crosswalk if one were present. After stopping, look in all directions for crossing vehicles and pedestrians and yield the right-of-way before moving into the intersection, because a stop sign always means a stop and then yielding.

lines.text: Triangle: slow and let traffic cross
Center lane for left turns, one-way follows the arrow

narration.text: To close, a stop sign is a red octagon with white letters. Stop behind the stop line, or behind the crosswalk, or where neither exists, at the closest point where you can see both ways without entering cross traffic, then look in all directions and yield. A yield sign is a downward red and white triangle with red letters, and it means slow down and let right-of-way traffic cross before you enter. The Shared Center Lane Left Turn Only lane is for left turns from either direction, and on a one-way street you never drive against the arrow.

You will also learn how route number signs show the type of road, how to read South Carolina's Secondary System Road Marker, where to find secondary roads on a map and what the Evacuation Route sign marks during a hurricane.

Interstate, US, state, city, county, local

narration.text: The shape and color of a route number sign show the type of road it marks: interstate, US, state, city, county or local. To use them well, plan a trip with a road map or a GPS device, then follow the route signs during the trip so you do not get lost in an unfamiliar area. Knowing the shape of each route sign lets you confirm at a glance that you are still on the type of road you planned to take. Each route sign shape marks a different type of road.

lines.text: S, then county number, then road number
Each county numbers its own roads

narration.text: South Carolina marks secondary roads with the Secondary System Road Marker. On that marker, the number right after the letter S tells you which county the road lies in, and the final number identifies the road itself. Every county has its own separate set of secondary road numbers. On the S road marker the county number comes first and the road number comes last, and each county keeps its own separate set of secondary road numbers. So the same road number can be used again in a different county, which is why the county number on the marker matters.

lines.text: Do not read the first number as the road

narration.text: Here is the trap. Drivers who see two numbers on the S road marker often assume the first one is the road number. It is not. The number right after the letter S tells you which county the road lies in, and the final number identifies the road itself. On the S road marker the county number comes first and the road number comes last. Because every county has its own separate set of secondary road numbers, reading the numbers in the wrong order can send you to a different road altogether. Read the marker as S, county, then road.

Secondary system roads are local roads serving rural and urban traffic. In rural areas they are not meant as through routes for drivers unfamiliar with the area. For through travel, stay on the main routes shown on the state map.

In this unit you will learn what the manual's yellow and white marking diagrams show, how passing is shown on two-direction roadways, and which other lane controls the manual pictures. Markings work together with signs and signals, so reading them correctly matters on every drive.

Pavement markings are lines, arrows, words or symbols painted on the road surface to give directions or warnings. They have several jobs. They divide lanes, show when you may pass or change lanes, show which lanes to use for turns, define pedestrian walkways and show where to stop for signs or signals. So a single stretch of road can carry several messages at once: a center line that tells you about passing, turn arrows that tell you which lane to use, a crosswalk that marks where pedestrians cross and a stop line that tells you exactly where to stop.

The manual's yellow lane marking diagrams all show two-direction roadways. On two-direction roadways the diagrams show passing prohibited in both directions, passing permitted, and passing permitted only when the dashed line is on your side. The white lane marking diagram shows a one-direction roadway on which passing is permitted. So the color of the line tells you about the traffic next to you: yellow markings appear where traffic moves in two directions, and white markings appear on a roadway where all traffic moves in one direction.

Knowing the exact stopping point keeps you out of crosswalks and cross traffic.

narration.text: A crosswalk defines the area where pedestrians may cross the roadway, and the manual pictures three common types of crosswalk markings. In this unit you will learn where to stop when a sign or signal requires it, what to do when there is no stop line and no crosswalk, your duty to yield to pedestrians, what to do where crosswalks are not marked, and which marking you obey first when both a stop line and a crosswalk are present. These rules protect people on foot, who are most at risk at intersections. You must yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk or entering one.

lines.text: Behind the stop line or crosswalk

narration.text: When a sign or signal makes you stop, stop behind the stop line or crosswalk. If there is neither, stop at the nearest point where you can see both ways without entering cross traffic. With no stop line and no crosswalk, the stopping point is the spot nearest the intersection where you can see both ways without moving into cross traffic. So the painted markings come first, and only when they are missing do you choose the stopping point yourself, always before the cross traffic and always where you can see in both directions.

lines.text: Yield to anyone in or entering

narration.text: You must yield to pedestrians who are in a crosswalk or entering one. That duty does not depend on whether the crosswalk is painted. Not every crosswalk is marked, so watch for pedestrians at intersections, and if no crosswalk is apparent, stop before entering the intersection. A crosswalk defines the area where pedestrians may cross the roadway, so a pedestrian stepping off the curb at an intersection may be entering a crosswalk even when there are no lines. Look for people on foot at every intersection, painted or not, and yield to them.

lines.text: Stop line before crosswalk: stop at the line

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a stop line is painted before a crosswalk, some drivers roll up to the crosswalk edge instead. But where a stop line comes before a crosswalk, the stop line must be obeyed first. When a stop line and a crosswalk are both present and the stop line comes first, you stop at the stop line rather than at the crosswalk. Stopping at the line keeps the crosswalk clear for pedestrians and gives you a better view of them as they cross. The line is there to set your stopping point, so treat it as the place to stop.

The manual pictures three common types of crosswalk markings. Whatever the pattern, a crosswalk defines the area where pedestrians may cross the roadway, and you must yield to pedestrians who are in it or entering it. Not every crosswalk is marked at all, so watch for pedestrians at intersections even where no pattern is painted. When a sign or signal makes you stop, you stop behind the stop line or crosswalk, and where a stop line comes before the crosswalk, the stop line must be obeyed first, keeping the whole marked crossing area clear.

Here is a quick check: you are stopping for a red light, and a stop line is painted before the crosswalk. Which do you obey first? The answer is the stop line. Where a stop line comes before a crosswalk, the stop line must be obeyed first, so you stop at the stop line rather than at the crosswalk. If there were no stop line, you would stop behind the crosswalk, and with neither, at the nearest point where you can see both ways without entering cross traffic. And you must always yield to pedestrians in or entering a crosswalk.

lines.text: Yield to pedestrians, marked or not

narration.text: To close, a crosswalk defines where pedestrians may cross, and the manual pictures three common types of crosswalk markings. You must yield to pedestrians in or entering a crosswalk, and because not every crosswalk is marked, watch for pedestrians at intersections and stop before entering when no crosswalk is apparent. When a sign or signal makes you stop, stop behind the stop line or crosswalk, obeying a stop line first when it comes before the crosswalk, and with neither, stop at the nearest point where you can see both ways without entering cross traffic.
